title: Bartok's pride and refusal of help
summary: Hammond and Goodman tried to help Bartok secretly; he took no charity.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong

blocks.x: By the way, you mentioned something about Bartok the other day and I'd like you to clarify that, because it doesn't sound like Bartok to me.
You said Bartok made a statement that he didn't want to write unless he got money for it; that doesn't sound like Bartok.
I'm trying to think; I read this somewhere years ago.
Maybe an assignment, but I don't think even that.
I don't think the money was the object. I think the point was that he wanted to write specific pieces because somebody wanted them and wanted to perform them, as opposed just to writing,
as opposed to being a manuscript paper collector, to writing pieces and sticking them in the draw and not having a performance for them.
I understand that. I understand it personally very well, but you know, you may be right. I'm just questioning it because he wouldn't teach composition; he would teach piano but not composition.
Well apparently Koussevitsky, not long before Bartok died, got him to write "Concerto for Orchestra" for the Boston Symphony.
I remember that very well. I heard the first performance of that.
I remember when he was at Columbia and I remember Benny and John Hammond, people of that group, György Sandor, trying to help Bartok, and he wouldn't permit it. He had a pension from

I know that Benny and John and that group tried to help him, but they had to do it in such a way that he wasn't aware of it. He was strangely proud about that sort of thing, he wouldn't accept it. He thought it was denegrading.
In Hungary he was sort of the dean of his country's composers; right?
So I guess to be forced out of a position like that is a very hard thing to accept.
